texte.ad35b2176800: You are playing Black in the Smith-Morra Gambit and are a pawn up after {z1} ({v1}). Use the counting aid from Table 3.2 to fill in a factor balance: what does White's compensation consist of? And what is your most important task now?
texte.b96806f8b4b3: Material: Black is a pawn ahead. Time: it is equal, because although White has the knight on c3 in play and Black has no piece out yet, Black is to move and draws level with the next piece move. King safety: {c1} for both. Both kings are still in the center, but they are not threatened. Activity ({c2} for White): the pawn on e4 stands in the center, and Black has no pawn there. The c-file is open, the queen on d1 already eyes d7 along the d-file, which is half-open for White, and every white piece that now comes into play immediately finds a free path, for example the bishop on f1 via c4 with f7 as its target. So the compensation lies in activity. White only gets a lead in time if Black does not put the moves into piece moves. Your most important task is therefore not to take more material, but to develop your pieces and bring your king to safety. If you keep the pawn along the way, that is a bonus, and it is no disaster if you have to give it back for healthy development. Remember: against a gambit, you develop first, because the extra pawn will not run away.
texte.71bf7c89545a: For the pawn, White has activity: the pawn on e4 in the center, open c- and d-files, a free path for every piece. As Black, your most important task is therefore development and king safety, not more material.
texte.75482fee257b: If you play the Scotch Game with White, you can choose {z2} instead of {z1}: the Göring Gambit. Which gambit from this chapter does the position resemble if Black accepts with {z3}, and is the sacrifice then real? With which move can Black take the sting out of the gambit without taking more material?
texte.fff23da07077: After {z1}, the same idea arises as in the Danish Gambit and the Smith-Morra Gambit: White gives a pawn and gets a developed knight, open files and a free path for both bishops in return. The sacrifice is real, because White does not simply win the pawn back. The simplest reply, however, is {z2}: Black attacks the pawn on e4 at once. After {z3}, material is equal, the black queen stands in the center, and with {z4} Black continues developing and attacks the knight on f3, which defends d4. As in the King's Gambit with {z5}, the counterthrust in the center takes away the lead in time that the gambit lives on. Remember: the counterthrust {z6} gives back material in the center and takes away the gambit's lead in time.
texte.c6a20d54556c: After 4... dxc3 5. Nxc3, a real gambit arises, like the Danish or the Smith-Morra Gambit. Simpler is 4... d5: Black attacks e4, gives back material in the center and takes away White's lead in time, which the gambit lives on.
texte.fe9ceff31b9e: For the position after {z1} in the Volga Gambit ({v1}), draw up a factor balance yourself from Black's point of view. Compare it with the balance after {z2} ({v2}): which factor has been added, and which has stayed the same? And why does that make the Volga Gambit longer-lasting than the King's Gambit?
texte.2e13f5fcea40: After {z1}: Material: White is a pawn ahead. Time: Black is two pieces ahead. The knight on f6 and the bishop on a6 are in play, White has not moved a piece yet, and because White is to move, the lead counts as it is. King safety {c1} for both, because both kings are still in the center. Activity {c2} for Black (half-open a- and b-files against a2 and b2, where the rooks will soon arrive). After {z2}, the black king is safe; {c3} has become {c4}. What has stayed the same is the pressure on a2 and b2 and the lead in time: two pieces against none have become three against one. Castling has added the rook on f8, while White has brought only the knight on c3 into play. This is exactly the difference from the King's Gambit: there, the compensation lives on time, which is used up after a few moves, whereas in the Volga Gambit it lives on open files and fixed targets that remain. Remember: compensation from the pawn structure lasts longer than compensation from time.
texte.1d456bd1a832: After 5... Bxa6, Black is a pawn down but has time and pressure on the half-open a- and b-files. Later king safety is added, while the pressure remains: this compensation lasts longer than the pure time of the King's Gambit.
texte.e53afd701e49: If you play {z1} with White, you will meet not only the Latvian Gambit but also the Elephant Gambit: with {z2}, Black offers the d-pawn. After {z3}, the pawn attacks the knight on f3, and White replies with {z4}. Why may Black not capture the knight with {z5} now? Draw up a factor balance for the position after {z6}: what has Black got for the pawn? And why is {z7} not an “premature queen” in the sense of Chapter 1?
texte.5e5a582878eb: After {z1}, the white queen stands on the e-file in front of the black king, and the squares e5, e6 and e7 are empty. The pawn on e4 is therefore absolutely pinned to the king on e8: {z2} is not even allowed, because Black's own king would then be in check. The balance: Material: White is a pawn ahead (d5). Time: White is one piece ahead. The knight on f3 and the queen on e2 are in play, Black has not moved a piece yet and is to move. That leaves a lead of one piece. King safety: {c1} for both, because both kings are in the center, and the black one also stands on the white queen's file. Activity: {c2} for White, because the queen pins the pawn on e4, and White attacks it a second time with {z3}. Black has {c3}: the pawn on e4 is far advanced but pinned, so Black has got hardly anything for the pawn. After {z4}, White is even two pawns up. In return, Black is better developed and presses against e4 with {z5} and {z6}, but White develops with {z7} and {z8}, castles queenside and is better. The early queen here is not an “premature queen” in the sense of Chapter 1: that deadly sin means a queen that is chased by the opponent's minor pieces and gives away tempi in the process. Black cannot attack the queen on e2 with tempo right away, and it fulfills a concrete task, the pin. Remember: an early queen is only premature if the opponent can chase it with tempo.
texte.a28e3dfeb02b: After 4. Qe2, the pawn on e4 is absolutely pinned to the king, so 4... exf3 is not even allowed. Black has got hardly anything for the pawn, and the queen on e2 is not premature, because it cannot be chased with tempo and it holds the pin.
texte.6319e14e2fdf: Classify the following four pawn offers from this chapter as a real sacrifice or a pseudo-sacrifice, and justify each answer in one sentence: the Queen's Gambit ({z1}), the Danish Gambit ({v1}), the Smith-Morra Gambit ({v2}) and the Budapest Gambit ({v3}).
texte.88aa3770cd3d: The Queen's Gambit is a pseudo-sacrifice: White wins the pawn back with {z1} and {z2}. The Danish Gambit is real: two pawns stay gone unless Black gives them back voluntarily. The Smith-Morra Gambit is real: one pawn stays gone, and White plays for development and open files. The Budapest Gambit lies in between: Black often wins the pawn back, but has to play accurately and aim the pieces deliberately at e5 to do so. So it is a real sacrifice with a good prospect of winning the material back. Remember: with every pawn offer, first ask whether the material comes back by itself.
texte.fa2a51c49975: The Queen's Gambit is a pseudo-sacrifice, because the pawn comes back with e3 and Bxc4. The Danish and the Smith-Morra Gambit are real sacrifices for development and open files; the Budapest Gambit lies in between, because Black often wins the pawn back, but only with accurate play.

On top of that, White is left with the isolated pawn on a2, a lasting weakness in the pawn structure (Chapter 5, Section 5.4).
